subject: Mechanical Engineering
title: Heat Treatment: Changing Properties with Fire
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Heat Treatment: Changing Properties with Fire.

hook.text: A blacksmith heats steel red-hot and quenches it in water. In seconds, soft iron becomes hard enough to cut stone.

buildup.text: Heating steel above 727°C transforms its crystal structure from ferrite to austenite. Carbon atoms dissolve into the lattice.

discovery.text: Quenching traps carbon in place, forming martensite — a super-hard but brittle phase. The atoms can't rearrange in time.

twist.text: Martensite is too brittle for tools. Tempering reheats it gently to release some hardness and restore toughness. Balance is key.

climax.text: Annealing does the opposite — slow cooling softens the metal for machining. Heat treatment tailors properties to the application.

punchline.text: Same steel, different heat, different metal. Temperature is the invisible alloy.

quiz.question: Why is quenched steel tempered after hardening?
options: To make it even harder by trapping more carbon atoms
Quenched martensite is too brittle — tempering restores toughness at the cost of some hardness
To change the steel's color for aesthetic purposes
